SpaceX Filing Gives Elon Musk the Final Word on Tesla Merger He Says He’s Staying Out Of

Elon Musk recused himself from the SpaceX-Tesla merger talks. His company's SEC filing suggests that doesn't mean much.

SpaceX's October 22 10-Q disclosed that any potential combination with Tesla "would be subject to further approval by our special committee, our board of directors and our controlling shareholder." Musk controls roughly 85% of SpaceX's voting power. He is the controlling shareholder.

Myriad: How low will Tesla stock go? Click to make your prediction.

Both companies formed special committees on October 20 to evaluate a proposed deal analysts estimate could create a combined entity worth around $3.5 trillion. Musk described staying out of the talks as "an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking, and I can't be in the conversation." The filing language suggests he'll have the last word anyway.

He's also already been in the conversation. Reuters reported that Musk's public endorsement of the deal earlier this month created a "mess" for the independent process, with insiders saying it complicated the special committees' ability to negotiate at arm's length.

Critics are pointing to Tesla's 2016 SolarCity acquisition—another conflicted transaction that cleared Delaware courts—as the closest governance precedent. SpaceX's own investor disclosures have flagged Musk's overlapping interests as a material risk.

Tesla shareholders must clear a 50%-of-all-outstanding-shares threshold—not a simpler majority of votes cast—a standard Musk himself called "quite a high hurdle." REX Financial estimates the merged company would give him roughly 57% of combined voting power.

Tesla's annual meeting is December 3.

Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ: RIVN) trades around $12 per share, giving the electric vehicle manufacturer a market capitalization of about $18 billion. That's a fraction of Tesla's valuation, but Rivian still has a long way to go before achieving consistent profitability.

Still, with production accelerating and its lower-priced R2 SUV now reaching customers, Rivian could look a lot different five years from now. My prediction? A $5,000 investment today could be worth approximately $10,000 by 2031.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The R2 could transform Rivian's business

Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in the third quarter, up about 45% year over year. Management also reaffirmed its full-year delivery guidance of 65,000 to 70,000 vehicles. Worth noting: much of Rivian's future growth depends on the R2.

Unlike Rivian's more expensive R1 SUV, the R2 is designed to appeal to a much broader market. Initial versions start around $58,000, with a lower-priced standard version clocking in at $45,000 in 2027. Higher production volumes should also help Rivian spread its manufacturing costs across more vehicles, potentially improving profitability. But Rivian's ambitions extend beyond selling electric vehicles, too.

Image source: Getty Images.

The company recently landed a deal with Uber Technologies involving an initial 10,000 autonomous R2 vehicles, with an option for another 40,000. Uber also agreed to invest up to $1.25 billion in Rivian through 2031, contingent on certain milestones.

Rivian's existing software business has been growing, too. The segment generated $515 million in Q2 revenue, with a gross margin of 42%. Its partnership with Volkswagen also provides another avenue to monetize vehicle software and electrical architecture.

What could $5,000 become?

Rivian shares closed at $12.34 on Oct. 19. At that price, a $5,000 investment would purchase approximately 405 shares. My five-year target is $25 per share. Here's how I arrive at that number.

The EV maker should be able to grow annual deliveries to 250,000 vehicles by 2031. This is a reasonable target considering the company's manufacturing expansion, which should push combined annual production capacity to 515,000 vehicles across its Illinois and Georgia facilities. Assuming an average selling price of $50,000, those deliveries would generate approximately $12.5 billion in automotive revenue.

Here are Investing.com's stocks of the week:

Cybersecurity stocks

Cybersecurity names were among the week's strong performers after an emergency security update for PHP, the programming language used by roughly 70% of websites worldwide, triggered a global alert.

Two critical vulnerabilities disclosed this week could allow hackers to take remote control of affected servers.

The incident highlights a growing challenge, with artificial intelligence accelerating the discovery of software weaknesses while potentially making them easier to exploit.

Okta led the moves with a 14% gain over the week, followed by Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike, both up 11%, and Cloudflare, up 9%.

Meta Platforms

Meta fell 7% on Thursday and is down 9.1% over the week after Wednesday's post-close results, with a surprise plan to issue a new class of non-voting stock overshadowing stronger-than-expected third-quarter revenue.

The company's special committee said in its filing that the move was motivated not only by keeping CEO Mark Zuckerberg in California but also by "an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital," citing recent and anticipated raises at Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI to fund the same AI growth.

The committee added that while Meta has sufficient resources for current needs, it would be prudent to act before more companies absorb available capital in the market. The Class C shares are intended for equity offerings from time to time and could be available as early as the end of 2026.

Tesla and SpaceX

Tesla gained 4.6% over the week, and SpaceX added 0.6% after both reported results and confirmed they are examining a tie-up.

What Happened?

Elon Musk is tying his companies Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) and SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) closer to Washington while spending record sums on the 2026 midterms.

CNBC reports he has committed about $366 million across at least 40 races, which makes him the biggest individual donor so far.

At least $276 million of it has gone to Republican groups and his own America PAC since July.

His companies are also leaning on federal money. FedScout says SpaceX has won at least $6.78 billion in federal work so far this year, nearly twice its 2024 total of $3.8 billion.

Tesla has its own stakes in Washington as Congress and federal agencies can change EV tax breaks, battery subsidies, autonomous vehicle rules, and trade policy.

Musk is also close to the White House again. In recent weeks, he sat beside President Trump at an AI summit and also received the National Medal of Science.

On Sept. 30, the Pentagon named him co-lead of Project Meridian.

What the Market Is Telling Us About Tesla Stock

Tesla's autonomy plans depend on regulators.

On its Q3 call, management said Robotaxi growth may shift from a technology issue to a regulatory one in Q1 and Q2. Elon Musk also said Tesla could be stopped by governments in some places.

The business itself looks strong. Tesla delivered over 480,000 vehicles for a second straight quarter and auto margins excluding credits rose from 16.3% to 18.1%.

Energy gross margin hit 33.1%, helped by tariff refunds and warranty true-downs.

Tesla now expects about $20 billion in capital spending this year. It also secured capacity to borrow up to $30 billion but does not plan to draw on it this calendar year.

For Tesla stock, the question is how long Musk's political goodwill lasts. His influence faded fast after a 2025 feud with Trump, and now he is back in the President's inner circle.

Investors in Tesla stock may want to watch November's election, and the result could shape the rules Tesla works under.

For now, Tesla stock is still tied to FSD demand, Robotaxi growth, and rising costs.
